concept.name: Know your customer
concept.definition: The set of procedures by which financial institutions verify the identity of customers and understand the nature of their activities, anchored in the U.S. by Section 326 of the USA PATRIOT Act (31 U.S.C. § 5318(l)), which requires minimum standards for verifying the identity of persons opening accounts, maintaining verification records, and screening against government lists of known or suspected terrorists.
concept.intuition: Before a firm lets you move money or trade, it must actually know who you are — name, address, ID documents — so criminals can't hide behind anonymous accounts.
concept.mechanics: At account opening the institution collects identifying information (name, date of birth, address, identification number), verifies it through documents or non-documentary methods, keeps the records, and checks the customer against government watchlists. KYC is supplemented by customer due diligence (CDD), including beneficial-ownership identification for legal entities and ongoing monitoring proportionate to risk.
concept.failure_modes: Verification relies on documents and databases that can be forged or stale, and shell structures can obscure beneficial owners; overly rigid KYC also excludes legitimate customers lacking standard IDs, and box-ticking programs can pass exams while missing genuinely suspicious relationships.
concept.misconceptions: KYC is not a one-time ID check at signup — regulators expect ongoing due diligence and monitoring commensurate with customer risk; nor is it merely a brokerage rule — it is a statutory Bank Secrecy Act obligation across financial institutions.
concept.example: A broker-dealer opening an account for a new customer collects her passport and Social Security number, verifies them against a database, screens her against OFAC lists, and records the verification before enabling trading.
